extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, NIH peer reviewers, and institutional sponsored programs staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how NIH Scientific Review Groups (SRGs) conduct the first-level peer review of grant applications, including reviewer roles, review criteria, scoring, and post-review products (summary statements, appeals). Intended to explain standards used to evaluate NIH grant applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the overall impact that your proposed project (or resource, or training, or center, etc.) will likely have on the biomedical research field(s) involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact scores reflect the reviewers’ overall assessment of the likelihood for the project to exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field(s) involved. Each reviewer gives a preliminary Overall Impact score prior to the meeting; for discussed applications, eligible panelists give final Overall Impact scores and the mean of final impact scores is multiplied by 10 to produce a final score ranging from 10 (high impact) through 90 (low impact). Preliminary scores are often used to determine which applications will be discussed. Not Discussed (ND) applications receive no numerical final Overall Impact score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scored Review Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Each grant application submitted to NIH is evaluated according to established review criteria that must be stated clearly in a notice of funding opportunity. Reviewers assign individual criterion scores for all scored review criteria; these scored criteria contribute to the Overall Impact score of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion scores typically use a numerical scale of 1 to 9 (1 = exceptional; 9 = poor) in whole numbers (no decimals). Each reviewer uses their own judgment to determine how each criterion weighs into the Overall Impact score unless the funding opportunity specifies otherwise. Some review criteria for particular FOAs may be re-defined or additional criteria added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Review Criteria (e.g., human subjects, animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional review criteria do not receive individual criterion scores but contribute to the Overall Impact score. Some of these criteria need to be considered acceptable before the NIH can award a grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include protections for human subjects, vertebrate animals, and biohazards. Reviewers are asked to make recommendations concerning protections for human subjects; inclusion (women, minorities, children); welfare of vertebrate animals; and other applicable areas. These criteria must sometimes be judged acceptable for award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Review Considerations (programmatic issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional review considerations do not receive individual criterion scores and do not contribute to the Overall Impact score. They provide input on programmatic issues that do not directly reflect scientific/technical merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include whether an application’s budget is sufficiently justified, or whether the project could be completed for a smaller budget or in fewer years than requested. They are used to seek expert input on programmatic matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale and calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most review criteria and the Overall Impact are rated using numerical scoring on a 9-point scale (1 = exceptional; 9 = poor). Final Overall Impact scores are determined by averaging final impact scores from all eligible members and multiplying the average by 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores use whole numbers only (no decimals). Preliminary scores are provided by assigned reviewers before the meeting and can be used to triage discussion. For each discussed application, eligible panelists provide a final Overall Impact score; the mean multiplied by 10 yields a 10–90 overall score. Percentiles may be provided to rank an application's impact relative to others in the SRG across review rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assignment and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO assigns at least three reviewers to assess each application and gives all reviewers on the panel (except those with conflicts) access to the applications to be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the meeting, assigned reviewers read each application thoroughly, write a critique summarizing strengths and weaknesses, and assign a preliminary Overall Impact score. At the meeting, the primary reviewer presents the application, the other assigned reviewers may provide additional comments, and all non-conflicted panelists discuss and score the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are recruited based on scientific and technical qualifications and other considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection considerations include: authority in their scientific field; dedication to high quality, fair, and objective reviews; ability to work collegially in a group setting; and balanced expertise appropriate for the applications under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific Review Officer (SRO) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO is the NIH extramural staff scientist and designated federal official responsible for ensuring objective and fair initial peer review and that applicable laws, regulations, and policies are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRO duties include assigning reviewers, managing conflicts of interest, actively managing the meeting for fair and effective review, ensuring compliance with review policy, and preparing a resume of discussion for all discussed applications to accurately reflect score-driving elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The chair serves as moderator of the discussion of scientific and technical merit of the applications under review and also serves as a peer reviewer for the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chair facilitates discussions and helps lead the SRG in considering scientific and technical issues during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer duties and expected behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must declare conflicts of interest, receive access to applications approximately six weeks prior to the meeting, maintain confidentiality, prepare written critiques, assign numerical scores to scored review criteria, and make recommendations on scientific and technical merit and applicable protections/inclusion/budget issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are trained and oriented by NIH; they should provide objective, fair, and timely reviews free from inappropriate influences. Reviewers should avoid divulging information outside the meeting and follow NIH guidance on human subjects protection, inclusion, stem cells, vertebrate animals, and budget information for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest management
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers declare conflicts of interest with specific applications and are managed according to NIH guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any reviewer with a conflict of interest is asked to leave the room before the group begins reviewing an individual application. The SRO documents and manages conflicts of interest and follows the Managing Conflict of Interest in NIH Peer Review guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and applicant contact restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH review meetings are confidential and reviewers are reminded not to divulge any information outside the meeting. Applicants may not contact reviewers to influence outcomes or try to access protected review information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are consequences for applicants who contact reviewers, send information directly to a reviewer, or attempt to access protected review information. Applicants should contact the NIH Program Official after receiving their summary statement for guidance on fundability and next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Statement content and release timing
rubrics_metrics.description: After the meeting, all reviewed applications receive an impact score and a summary statement prepared by the SRO; NIH typically releases scores in eRA Commons within 3 business days and uploads the summary statement within about 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summary statement includes: Impact Score and Percentile (if applicable); Brief summary of the SRG discussion (written by the SRO); Criterion scores from the assigned reviewers; Bulleted critiques (strengths and weaknesses) from the assigned reviewer; Budget recommendations; Any administrative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Discussed (ND) determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications unanimously judged by the SRG to be less competitive (typically rank in the bottom half) are not discussed at the meeting and do not receive a numerical final Overall Impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ND status is used to triage applications; applicants whose applications are not discussed will still receive summary information but no final numeric overall impact score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals grounds for peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH's peer review appeal system allows investigators and applicant organizations to seek reconsideration of the initial review results if they believe the review process was flawed for specified reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid grounds include bias of a reviewer, conflict of interest, absence of appropriate expertise, or factual errors by one or more reviewers that could have substantially altered the review outcome. This appeals policy does not apply to appeals of funding decisions, MERIT award extension decisions, or technical evaluations of R&D contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review training and orientation expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH provides reviewers extensive orientation and training to ensure they are prepared for participation in SRGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orientation materials remind reviewers of confidentiality rules and other policies; NIH also vets reviewers for appropriate expertise, potential conflicts of interest, and other requirements based on NIH peer review policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget appropriateness review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may be asked to make recommendations concerning appropriateness of budget requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget recommendations appear in the summary statement; reviewers can comment whether the project could be completed with a smaller budget or fewer years, and these comments are treated as additional review considerations (do not directly affect Overall Impact score unless specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips for applicants about readability for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should prepare applications with the understanding that while assigned reviewers read carefully, many other reviewers may be scanning the application as they listen to the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you prepare your application, think about how to make it easy for someone scanning it to understand what you are proposing and find the information they are looking for. Applicants may suggest study section assignments via the PHS Assignment Request Form and use tools like the CSR Assisted Referral Tool.
